stages.title: Planning a Show
stages.description: A show starts with a story you can finish. Decide the format, the roles, and the plan before anyone presses record.
learningObjectives: Pick a format and an idea that fits your time and access
Split the work into producer, writer, host, and editor roles
Plan a structure and a list of the sounds you need
Write narration that sounds like talking, not reading

explainBack.question: You and two friends want to make a ten-minute episode about your town's oldest shop in three weeks. Explain how you would check that the idea works, how you would split the jobs, what you would plan before recording, and how you would write the narration.
rubric: Podcast formats vary widely, from interviews to narrated stories, and the format should fit the story
Check the idea is realistic: you can reach the people and places you need within the timeline
Split roles such as producer, writer, host, and editor
Plan the structure and list the sounds and interviews you need before recording
A script marks where narration and clips go
Narration should sound natural and energetic, like talking to a friend, with shorter sentences

resources.title: Starting Your Podcast: A Guide For Students
resources.description: NPR's step-by-step guide to planning, recording, and scripting a first podcast.
keyPoints: Podcast formats vary widely, and a smartphone plus a computer is enough to start
Divide the work into roles: producer, writer, host, and editor
Brainstorm, then check the idea is realistic and fits the timeline
Plan the structure and the list of sounds you need
Prepare interviews with research and open-ended questions, record somewhere quiet, and have the guest introduce themselves on tape
Script where narration and clips go, and write shorter sentences so the host sounds natural, like talking to a friend

stages.title: Microphones & the Room
stages.description: The microphone and the room shape the sound more than any later fix. Choose gear for your setup and treat the space around your voice.
learningObjectives: Compare USB microphones with an interface setup
Choose between dynamic and condenser microphones
Control pops, thumps, and room echo
Monitor with headphones and check the levels

explainBack.question: You will record weekly in a bedroom with bare walls. Explain what microphone type you would choose and why, how you would set it up, and what you would do to the room and your monitoring to get a clean recording.
rubric: A USB mic is simple but ties you to a computer and is awkward with several mics; an interface with XLR mics scales better
Dynamic mics reject more of the room; condensers are more sensitive and pick up more room sound
Use a stand that does not sit on the table and a pop filter to avoid thumps and plosives
Cut echo by covering hard surfaces and putting soft material such as blankets or clothes around and behind you
Wear closed headphones while recording
Hearing yourself through direct monitoring does not prove the computer is recording, so watch the input meters

resources.title: Podcasting Basics, Part 1: Voice Recording Gear
resources.author: Jeff Towne
resources.description: A public-radio guide to microphones, interfaces, headphones, and the recording space.
keyPoints: A podcast is an audio file delivered to subscribers through an RSS feed
USB mics are simple but limited to a computer, with weaker preamps and trouble running several mics at once
Direct monitoring lets you hear yourself, but only the input meters show the computer is actually recording
Dynamic mics have lower output and reject the room better; condensers are hotter and pick up more room sound
Avoid table stands that pass on thumps, and use a mesh pop filter
Wear closed headphones, put soft material behind you as well as behind the mic, and remember the mic is the biggest factor in final sound

resources.title: How To Sound Great | Student Podcast Challenge Guide To Sound | NPR
resources.description: NPR producers show cheap ways to make a room sound better.
keyPoints: Hard, bare surfaces make a recording echo
Covering hard surfaces with soft material cuts the echo
A pillow fort or a closet full of clothes is a cheap recording booth
Listen to a test recording before the real one

stages.title: Recording Interviews
stages.description: A good interview is a prepared conversation with a well-placed microphone. Put the guest at ease, get close, and stay quiet while they talk.
learningObjectives: Prepare for a guest's role in the story
Set the guest at ease with the equipment
Place the microphone to avoid pops and room noise
Get every answer you need in one session

explainBack.question: You are about to interview a nervous local expert in their kitchen. Explain how you would prepare, set up the room and microphone, put them at ease, and run the conversation so the tape is usable.
rubric: Prepare by thinking about the guest's role in the story and what you want from the conversation
Remove noise first: unplug noisy appliances and silence phones
Set levels and do a test run; get the mic close and slightly off-axis to avoid plosive pops
Make the mic feel normal by handling it casually and keeping it below eye level
Start with light conversation, and ask the expert to explain as if you know nothing
Stay quiet while they answer, wait until they finish, and ask everything now because a later phone call will sound different

resources.title: Feign ignorance, demystify the mic and other audio interview tips
resources.description: NPR Training's advice for preparing guests and getting a usable audio interview.
keyPoints: Prepare by thinking about the role each source will play in the story, but leave room to be surprised
Make the equipment less daunting by handling it casually before the interview
Keep the mic below eye level and stop checking the equipment mid-conversation
Start with light conversation instead of grilling the source
Feign ignorance so experts explain simply for listeners
Treat it as the only chance to talk, because a phone follow-up sounds different from the original tape

resources.title: Hunting For Sound | Student Podcast Challenge Guide To Sound | NPR
resources.description: NPR producers on microphone pickup patterns, placement, and gathering sound.
keyPoints: A cardioid mic picks up mostly what is in front of it; an omni mic picks up all around
Set levels and do a test run before the interview
Get close to the speaker and angle the mic to cut plosive pops
Stay quiet and wait until the subject has finished speaking

stages.title: Choosing Editing Software
stages.description: The right editor depends on how many voices and layers your show has. Learn what separates a simple recorder from a multitrack workstation.
learningObjectives: Decide when a simple recorder is enough
Explain what a multitrack DAW adds
Contrast destructive and non-destructive editing
Name editing tools built for spoken word

explainBack.question: A friend asks which free or cheap software to edit a weekly two-host show with music and sound effects. Explain the difference between a simple recorder and a multitrack editor, what destructive editing means, and which tools you would consider.
rubric: A simple recorder or editor suits one or two voices with little layering
A multitrack DAW lets you place voices, music, and effects on separate tracks and mix them
Destructive editing changes the audio file itself; non-destructive editing keeps the original and can be undone
Audacity is free and cross-platform but edits destructively
GarageBand is free on Macs; Hindenburg is built for spoken word with loudness tools

resources.title: Podcast Basics Part 2: Software
resources.author: Jeff Towne
resources.description: A comparison of recording and editing software for spoken-word shows.
keyPoints: Simple recording apps are enough for one or two voices
A multitrack DAW is needed when you layer voices, music, and effects
Audacity is free but uses destructive editing
GarageBand comes free with Macs and handles multitrack work
Hindenburg was designed by radio people and can normalise loudness on export

stages.title: Levels, Loudness & Processing
stages.description: Peaks are not loudness. Clean the recording, compress it gently, and set the whole episode to a consistent loudness target.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between peak level and loudness
Set a loudness target in LUFS for a podcast
Use gentle compression, a limiter, and a high-pass filter
Choose a sensible bitrate and file format for speech

explainBack.question: Your episode peaks near 0 dB, yet listeners say it is quieter than other shows and the guest is much louder than you. Explain why peak normalising did not fix it, and what processing and loudness target you would use instead.
rubric: Peak normalising only sets the loudest moment; it does not make the overall program loud or even
Loudness is measured in LUFS, and about -16 LUFS is a common podcast target
Gentle compression evens out levels between voices
A limiter on the master stops peaks from clipping
A high-pass filter removes rumble and some plosive pops; noise reduction can leave artifacts, so cut noise before recording
Mono speech can use a lower bitrate than stereo, and you export a full-quality WAV before encoding

resources.title: Podcasting Basics, Part 3: Audio Levels and Processing
resources.author: Jeff Towne
resources.description: How to get a podcast loud, even, and clean before it is encoded.
keyPoints: Eliminate noise before recording, because noise reduction leaves artifacts
Peak normalising does not equal loudness
Aim for about -16 LUFS for podcasts, louder than the -24 used in broadcast
Use gentle compression of a few dB and a limiter on the master to catch peaks
A high-pass filter cuts rumble and plosive pops
Mono files are half the size of stereo, and around 64 kbps MP3 works for mono speech; export WAV first, then encode

stages.title: Delivery Specs
stages.description: Podcast apps have published audio specs. Hit the loudness and peak target, and pick a codec and bitrate that players expect.
learningObjectives: State Apple's loudness and true-peak targets
Choose between AAC and MP3
Pick bitrates for mono and stereo shows
Explain why loudness is set before encoding

explainBack.question: You are about to export your first episode for Apple Podcasts. Explain the loudness and peak targets you would hit, the codec and bitrate you would choose for a mono interview show, and why you set loudness before encoding.
rubric: Aim for about -16 LKFS integrated loudness, within about 1 dB
Keep true peak at or below -1 dBFS
Set loudness before encoding, because encoding can raise peaks
AAC is recommended over MP3 for the same quality at a lower bitrate
Mono shows can use about 64 to 128 kbps and stereo about 128 to 256 kbps

resources.title: Audio requirements
resources.description: Apple's published loudness, codec, and bitrate guidance for podcast audio.
keyPoints: Target about -16 dB LKFS integrated loudness, within plus or minus 1 dB
Keep true peak at or below -1 dBFS, measured as in ITU-R BS.1770
Set loudness before encoding
AAC is recommended over MP3
Mono episodes use about 64 to 128 kbps and stereo about 128 to 256 kbps, at 44.1 or 48 kHz

stages.title: RSS, Hosting & Distribution
stages.description: A podcast is an audio file plus an RSS feed that points to it. A host stores both, and directories read the feed.
learningObjectives: Explain how an RSS feed and enclosure deliver episodes
List what a valid episode entry needs
Explain what a podcast host does
Validate a feed before submitting it

explainBack.question: A friend uploaded an MP3 to their website and asks why it is not showing up in podcast apps. Explain what an RSS feed is, what each episode entry needs, what a podcast host does, and what they should check before submitting to Apple Podcasts.
rubric: A podcast is an audio file plus an RSS (XML) feed; each episode is listed as an enclosure pointing to the file
The feed must be RSS 2.0 and publicly reachable, and the server must allow HEAD and byte-range requests
Each episode needs an enclosure with url, length, and type, and a GUID that never changes
A host stores the audio and feed, handles bandwidth, and provides statistics
Validate the feed before submitting; tags are case sensitive and characters like & must be escaped
Submitting to Apple needs a Podcasts Connect account, required tags, at least one episode, and cover art

resources.title: Podcasting Basics, Part 4: Hosting & Distribution
resources.author: Jeff Towne
resources.description: How RSS feeds, hosts, and directories fit together.
keyPoints: A podcast has two parts: the audio file and the XML (RSS) feed that lists it
The RSS enclosure that made podcasting possible appeared around 2003
Directories add their own tags, and players may only show a limited number of episodes
Keep the feed small and validate it before submitting
Hosts such as Libsyn, SoundCloud, Archive.org, or S3 store files, and hosts help with bandwidth and statistics

resources.title: Podcast RSS feed requirements
resources.description: Apple's technical rules for a feed it will accept.
keyPoints: The feed must be RSS 2.0 and publicly addressable
The server must support HEAD requests and byte-range requests
Each episode needs a unique enclosure with url, length, and type, and a GUID that never changes
Use ASCII file names, case-sensitive tags, RFC 2822 dates, and escape & as &
Submitting needs an Apple Podcasts Connect account, the required tags, at least one episode, and artwork

stages.title: Cover Art & Rights
stages.description: Cover art has to meet a spec to be listed, and every clip or song you use has to be yours to use. Fair use is a judgment, not a time limit.
learningObjectives: Meet the cover art size and file rules
Explain the four fair use factors
Explain why there is no safe number of seconds
Decide when to get permission instead

explainBack.question: You want to open each episode with 15 seconds of a popular song and use a film still in your cover art. Explain the cover art rules you would follow, how fair use is decided, and why "under 30 seconds is fine" is not a rule.
rubric: Cover art should be a square 3000 by 3000 pixel JPG or PNG
Cover art must not have transparency or an alpha channel
Fair use is decided case by case on four factors: purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market
Transformative use such as commentary or criticism favours fair use more than using a song as decoration
There is no fixed number of seconds or percentage that is automatically fair use
When in doubt, use licensed or original material, or get permission

resources.title: Show cover template
resources.description: Apple's size and file rules for podcast cover art.
keyPoints: Use a square image of 3000 by 3000 pixels
Submit JPG or PNG
Do not use transparency or an alpha channel
Do not use Apple logos or imply Apple endorsement

resources.title: U.S. Copyright Office Fair Use Index
resources.description: How U.S. law decides whether using someone else's work is fair use.
keyPoints: Fair use is weighed under Section 107 on four factors
Purpose and character: transformative, nonprofit, or educational uses are more likely to be fair
Nature of the work: using creative work is less likely to be fair than using factual work
Amount and substantiality: using the heart of a work weighs against fair use even if it is short
Effect on the market for the original
There is no set number of words, seconds, or percentage that is automatically fair use

name: Podcasting
description: Plan a show, record clean voices and interviews, edit and set loudness, export to spec, publish through an RSS feed, and use cover art and other people's material within the rules.
